questions.problem: A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are $5,$ $3,$ and $0,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $5,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=5\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{5}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{5}.$

questions.problem: A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=8,$ ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{5},$ and ${\sigma }_{3}=0,$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=8,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={8}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={8}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=8.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=8.$

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=8={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=5={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=8$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $9$ of ${A}^{T}A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=5={\sigma }_{1},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{1}={5}^{2}=25,$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=3={\sigma }_{2},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{2}={3}^{2}=9.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=9$ of ${A}^{T}A$ is ${v}_{2}.$
